Patient Vignette: Mr. A. (Age 80, South Asian Male, Widowed, Retired Coast Guard)

Mr. A. is a thin, dignified man who moves with the careful economy of someone who has spent a lifetime on a ship. He sits upright in the chair, hands resting on his knees, and he does not look at me when he speaks. His English is precise, but his voice is a low, gravelly hum, as if the words are being pulled from deep within a hold.

He begins, as he always does, with the sea. He joined the Indian Coast Guard in 1965, a young man from a coastal village who knew the temperament of the ocean better than most. He was a navigator, a man of charts and stars, responsible for the lives of his crew. He speaks of those years with a quiet, unassailable pride. He speaks of his wife, who passed seven years ago, as his "anchor." They had a quiet life, two sons, a small flat in Mumbai. It was a life of order and purpose.

The story he cannot tell, but which he has shown me in fragments over our sessions, begins on a moonless night in 1982. He was the officer on watch. A fishing trawler, unlit, drifted into their patrol path. He saw it too late. The order to turn the wheel came from his mouth, but the sea, the dark, the physics of a heavy vessel, had already made its decision. The Coast Guard cutter sliced through the smaller boat. He remembers the sound-not a crash, but a wet, splintering groan. He remembers the silence that followed, broken by a single, high-pitched cry from the water that was abruptly cut short. They pulled one survivor, a young fisherman, from the wreckage. The man's legs were crushed below the knee. Mr. A. helped carry the stretcher. He saw the man's face, contorted in pain, saw the blood pooling on the deck, saw the fisherman's eyes, wide and white in the dark, looking directly at him.

In the weeks that followed, he was cleared of any wrongdoing. The trawler was at fault. His superiors told him it was a tragedy, a part of the job. He nodded, filed the report, and went home to his wife. But he stopped sleeping. He would wake in a cold sweat, the sound of that splintering groan echoing in his ears. He began to avoid the sea. He took a desk job, citing his age. He stopped going to the beach with his sons, making excuses about the sun.

Now, at 80, the sea has followed him inland. He lives in a small, quiet apartment in a retirement community. He has a routine: he wakes at 4:00 AM, makes tea, and sits in the dark. He does this to avoid the dreams. The dreams are not of the crash itself, but of the fisherman's face. In the dream, the man is not in the water, but standing on Mr. A.'s deck, at the foot of his bed, his legs now whole, his eyes still wide and accusing. Mr. A. will not say the word "guilt." He says, instead, "I was the one with the chart. I was the one who should have seen."

His sons call him every Sunday. He answers, but he has little to say. He feels a vast, hollow distance from them, from all of life. He describes it as being wrapped in a thick, wet fog. He cannot feel joy, he says, only a terrible, heavy vigilance. He flinches at loud noises-a car backfiring, a pot clattering in the kitchen-and his heart will pound for hours. He has stopped reading the newspaper because the word "fishing" or "vessel" can trigger a full day of spiraling thoughts. He carries a small, smooth stone in his pocket. He does not know why. He says it helps him "feel something solid."

He came to me because his son, a doctor, insisted. He told me, "I am old. I have done my duty. But I am tired of carrying this." He is not looking for forgiveness. He is looking for a way to put the stone down. He is looking for a way to feel the sun on his face again without seeing the moonless night.
